title: Neural scaling law
summary:
In machine learning, a neural scaling law is an empirical scaling law that describes how neural network performance changes as key factors are scaled up or down. These factors typically include the number of parameters, training dataset size, and training cost. The test loss of well-trained neural networks often follows precise power-law scaling relations with either the size of the training dataset or the number of parameters in the network. Crucially, the best results often come when all three are scaled together in a balanced way. Simply making a model bigger without more data or training time can lead to underperformance.

The scenarios in which scaling behaviors were found include large-scale vision, language, audio, video, diffusion, generative modeling, multimodal learning, contrastive learning, AI alignment, robotics, out-of-distribution generalization, continual learning, transfer learning, and reinforcement learning, among many others. The architectures for which these scaling behaviors have been observed include residual neural networks, transformers, MLPs, MLP-mixers, recurrent neural networks, convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, U-nets, encoder-decoder models, mixture of experts models, and sparse pruned models.

Other than scaling up training compute, one can also scale up inference compute or test-time compute. As an example, the Elo rating of AlphaGo improves steadily as it is allowed to spend more time on its Monte Carlo Tree Search per play. For AlphaGo Zero, increasing Elo by 120 requires either 2x model size and training, or 2x test-time search.

Neural scaling laws were formalized in part by research from OpenAI, DeepMind, and other AI labs. Notably, the 2020 paper by OpenAI titled "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" systematically demonstrated how language model performance improves across many orders of magnitude. Researchers have proposed theories that explain the origins of and connect these scaling laws, identifying variance-limited and resolution-limited scaling behavior for both dataset and model size, for a total of four scaling regimes.
